corrected_value.authors: Gullo, K., Berger, J., Etkin, J., & Bollinger, B.
corrected_value.title: Does time of day affect variety-seeking?

decisions.location: Abstract, line 37 (and Background, lines 72-87; Method and Results, lines 96-185; Discussion, lines 188-198; References, lines 205-209)
decisions.quote: To shed light on the different findings, we carry out a replication using a unique dataset from the UK, which tracks individual purchases of food and drinks for out of home consumption over a period of three years. Similar to Gullo et al. (2019), we found variety-seeking increases from the morning to the afternoon. Additionally, we found a post-lunch dip. Our results as such lend further support to the matching mechanism between variety-seeking and diurnal level proposed by Gullo et al. (2019) rather than the compensating mechanism suggested by Roehm and Roehm (2004).
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. Luna triage mistakenly conflated target_index 1 (Gullo et al., 2019) with the sibling target Roehm and Roehm (2004) (shipped row '1493'). In fact, Trinh (2025) explicitly frames and conducts the study as an empirical replication designed to adjudicate the conflicting time-of-day variety-seeking findings of both Roehm and Roehm (2004) and Gullo, Berger, Etkin, and Bollinger (2019, Journal of Consumer Research 46(1):20-35, DOI 10.1093/jcr/ucy061). Specifically, Trinh (2025) retests Gullo et al.'s (2019) full-day (6 am to 11 pm) continuous non-linear diurnal pattern using polynomial regressions across three variety-seeking measures (brand count, Entropy, and reversed HHI; Figs. 1-3, Table 1), confirming Gullo et al.'s finding that variety-seeking increases from morning to early afternoon (6 am to 1 pm) and supporting Gullo et al.'s diurnal matching mechanism. The sole shipped row (input_row_index '1493', Roehm & Roehm, 2004, Marketing Letters 15:213-221, DOI 10.1007/s11002-005-0457-y) is a separate 2004 paper by different authors in a different journal reporting the opposite effect, so report equivalence does not apply and Gullo et al. (2019) is a genuinely absent replication target.
